Partial Covariance and the Spurious Response to Selection
metadata.display_heading: Partial Covariance and the Spurious Response to Selection

blocks.content: To express the selection response in terms of the Price equation, as done above, let $ z_i $ denote the phenotypic value of the $ i $th parent whose relative fitness is $ w_i $ and whose offspring have mean value $ \overline{z}_i $ and, hence, a parent-offspring deviation $ \bar{\delta}_i = \overline{z}_i - z_i $. Equation 6.7c shows the general expression for response as $$ R_{z}=\sigma(w_{i},\overline{z}_{i})+E(\overline{\delta}_{i}) $$

Heywood’s key insight is that Equation 6.30a can be decomposed into contributions from two biologically interpretable linear regressions and their corresponding residuals. The first regression involves offspring $ (z_i) $ and parental $ (z_i) $ values $$ \begin{array}{r l}{\overline{{z}}_{i}=\mu+\beta_{\overline{{z}}|z}z_{i}+e_{\overline{{z}},i},\quad\mathrm{w h e r e}\quad\beta_{\overline{{z}}|z}=\frac{\sigma(\overline{{z}}_{i},z_{i})}{\sigma_{z}^{2}}}\end{array} $$

The second is the regression of relative fitness $ w_{i} $ of a parent i on its phenotypic value $ z_{i} $ $$ w_{i}=1+\beta_{w|z}z_{i}+e_{w,i},\quad\mathrm{w h e r e}\quad\beta_{w|z}=\frac{\sigma(w_{i},z_{i})}{\sigma_{z}^{2}}=\frac{S}{\sigma_{z}^{2}} $$

It is important to stress that we are not assuming that the true relationship between either the mean offspring value $ \overline{z}_{i} $ or paternal fitness $ w_{i} $ and paternal phenotype value $ z_{i} $ is linear, but rather simply considering the best linear regression for these relationships and the resulting residuals.
